claims.text: HEAs possess intrinsic heterogeneous lattice distortion that creates spatially variable dislocation-pinning sites.
Variable dislocation pinning enhances dynamic strain hardening in HEAs under high-strain-rate deformation relative to conventional alloys.
The proposed HEA samples have a disordered solid-solution structure.
The baseline alloy has lower configurational entropy than the HEA while having similar overall composition and yield strength.
Multi-element alloying produces spatially varying lattice distortions in the HEA.
Local lattice distortions impede dislocation motion.
Severe and spatially variable lattice distortions act as dislocation-pinning centers.
Under high-strain-rate deformation, lattice-distortion barriers increase the activation energy required for dislocation glide.
The increased barrier to dislocation glide raises the dynamic strain-hardening rate.
The proposed mechanism enables HEAs to retain higher strength without a proportional loss of ductility relative to alloys with less pronounced lattice distortion.
At high strain rates, HEAs will exhibit a higher dynamic strain-hardening rate than the matched conventional baseline.
At high strain rates, HEAs will exhibit higher dynamic flow stresses than the matched conventional baseline.
Under quasi-static loading, the HEA and baseline may exhibit more comparable mechanical responses than under high-strain-rate loading.
The proposed mechanism is expected to hold primarily for HEAs with predominantly disordered solid-solution structures.
The proposed mechanism may not apply to HEAs containing substantial phase segregation or precipitation.
Processing routes that minimize lattice distortion, such as extreme annealing, may suppress the proposed mechanism.
Grain-boundary effects, texture, and residual stresses may also contribute to the observed dynamic response.
